To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
congenital factor X deficiency is a heterogeneous disorder that can be divided into two major categories: type I, in the absence of a CRM (antigen) and type II in the presence of a CRM.
Congenital factor X deficiency is commonly categorized as type I, with concomitant decreases in activity and antigen, and type II, with low activity and normal or near‐normal antigen.
Congenital factor X deficiency is commonly categorized in type I, in the case of a concomitant reduction of activity and antigen, and in type II when activity is low but the antigen is normal.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the study of the molecular basis of congenital factor X deficiency and its clinical consequences.
the molecular characterization of congenital Factor X deficiencies with a defective intrinsic and extrinsic system.
the study of the molecular biology of Factor X deficiency.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that

in the extrinsic defect there is no clear genotype‐phenotypes correlation, whereas in the intrinsic defect there seems to be a correlation with a mutation in exon 6 and a defect in the intrinsic and in the extrinsic systems.

in the case of type II congenital factor X deficiency, the defect can be in all three systems (extrinsic and intrinsic, as well as in the RVV dependent) or only in the intrinsic and extrinsic systems.
the classification of the congenital factor X deficiency into type I and type II is not adequate, and should be abandoned.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the classification of Factor X deficiency is still a challenge.
the classification of congenital factor X deficiencies should be revised.
the defects in Factor X deficiency are extremely heterogeneous.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the evaluation of congenital Factor X deficiencies should be based on the results of a multipronging approach.
the classification of congenital Factor X deficiency as either type I or type II is not sufficient.
the evaluation of patients with Factor X deficiency must include a multipronged analysis of the clotting, chromogenics, and immunological assays, in addition to the molecular biology analysis.
